subject: DI01000031

intro_text.en: Unit 1 of Communication Skills in English: what communication means and why the four language skills (LSRW) carry it, the seven-part model S + E + C + D + R + N + F, the upward and downward levels of an organisation, the verbal, non-verbal, visual, interpersonal, intrapersonal, extra personal and mass types, and the five families of barriers with the cure for each. Every rule is followed by worked examples, and fourteen answered practice questions are in section 7.

body.en:
Definition

Communication is the exchange of ideas, information or feelings between two or more people so that the receiver understands what the sender meant.

The key words are exchange (it goes both ways) and understands (the message has to arrive, not just leave).

One idea, many forms

SituationWhat is sentHow it travels
Supervisor tells a fitter to check the bearingan instructionspoken words
A notice on the workshop boarda safety rulewritten words
A red lamp on a machine panela warninga visual signal
A thumbs-up after a job is checkedapprovala gesture

Why a diploma engineer needs it

On site you will give instructions, read drawings, write reports, explain a fault and speak to a customer. Each of those is communication, and each can go wrong.

Examples of everyday messages

Short messages you already send

  • "Bring the 12 mm spanner." - instruction
  • "The motor is hot, stop the line." - warning
  • "Job finished at 4 pm." - information
  • "Well done, the alignment is perfect." - appreciation

Common mistake

Treating communication as 'sending'. If the receiver did not understand, the message did not happen.

The four skills

SkillWhat you doExample from a workshop
Listeningreceive and interpret speechfollowing a briefing before a shutdown
Speakingproduce speechexplaining a fault to the supervisor on the phone
Readinginterpret written textreading the maintenance manual and the drawing
Writingproduce written textwriting the job card entry and an e-mail to the vendor

Receptive and productive

Listening and reading are receptive (you take in); speaking and writing are productive (you put out). A balanced course practises all four.

Examples of each skill in one day

A technician's day

  • 7:30 - listens to the shift handover (listening)
  • 9:00 - reads the wiring diagram before opening the panel (reading)
  • 11:00 - tells the helper which tools to bring (speaking)
  • 4:30 - writes the breakdown entry in the log book (writing)

Common mistake

Calling listening 'hearing'. Hearing is passive; listening is active and takes attention.

h.en: 1.3 Listening is the skill that is used most

body.en:
Hearing and listening are different

Hearing is the ear receiving sound. Listening is paying attention, understanding and remembering.

Examples that show the difference

Same sound, different result

  • You hear the machine alarm but keep working - hearing only.
  • You hear the alarm, stop, and check the coolant level - listening.
  • You hear a customer say 'make it fast' and you speed up the wrong job - poor listening.
  • You repeat back 'so the 40 mm shaft is urgent, the rest later?' - active listening.

Three habits of a good listener

  1. Face the speaker and keep eye contact.
  2. Do not plan your reply while the other person is still talking.
  3. Repeat the key point back in your own words.

Common mistake

Nodding while thinking about something else. The nod is not evidence of understanding.

What employers notice first

Technical knowledge gets you the interview; clear communication keeps you on the team. The four skills appear in every job advertisement as 'good communication skills'.

Examples by situation

SituationSkill neededA good version
Client asks why the pump failedspeaking + explaining"The seal dried out during the shutdown; we have replaced it and run the pump for an hour."
Writing a daily reportwriting"Line 2 stopped 10:15-11:00 due to belt slip. Belt replaced, alignment checked."
Handover to the next shiftspeaking + listening"Panel 3 is on manual; do not reset until the vendor calls."
Reading a vendor's mailreadingnoticing that the delivery date changed from 5th to 12th

One example of a costly misunderstanding

"Grease the bearing weekly" is read as "grease the motor weekly". The bearing seizes, the motor survives. Twelve words, one breakdown.

Common mistake

Believing grammar alone is communication skill. Accuracy helps, but clarity and courtesy carry the message.

Three wrong ideas

  • "It means big words." No - "Please send the drawing" works better than "Kindly expedite the despatch of the requisite drawing."
  • "It is only speaking." No - a badly written e-mail can cost a contract before anyone speaks.
  • "It is fixed at birth." No - it is a skill, so it improves with practice and feedback.

Simple words, complete message

WordyClear
at this point in timenow
in the event thatif
utiliseuse
please revertplease reply

Examples of the same message at three levels

Asking for a report

  • Too blunt: "Send report."
  • Too heavy: "You are hereby requested to furnish the said report at the earliest."
  • Right: "Please send the line-2 report by Friday 5 pm."

Common mistake

Adding length to sound professional. Length hides the request; short sentences deliver it.

title.en: 2. Effective Communication and the Seven Cs

body.en:
The test

Communication is effective when the receiver's understanding matches the sender's intention, and the reply or action shows it.

Four conditions

  • A clear purpose - what should the reader or listener do next?
  • A suitable channel - a phone call for an urgent stop, an e-mail for a record.
  • Simple, correct language.
  • Feedback - a reply, a nod, a completed job, a signature.

Examples: effective and ineffective

MessageVerdictWhy
"Stop the conveyor, the guard is loose."effectiveone action, one reason, no doubt
"Something seems wrong with the machine, maybe check it."vagueno action, no machine named
"Meeting shifted to 3 pm, Room 4."effectivetwo facts, no padding
"As per discussion, needful will be done."uselessno one knows what will be done

Common mistake

Judging your own message by how much effort you put in. Judge it by what the receiver does next.

The checklist

A good message is clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete and courteous. Seven words, ten seconds, most misunderstandings prevented.

One example for each C

CWeakBetter
Clear"Do the needful.""Replace the gasket and refit the cover."
Concise"At this point of time we are not in a position to...""We cannot supply before Monday."
Concrete"The motor is faulty.""The motor draws 9 A against a rated 6 A."
Correct"The bolts is loose.""The bolts are loose."
Coherent"Belt replaced. Also the pump. Yesterday.""Yesterday we replaced the pump, then the belt."
Complete"Meeting on Monday.""Meeting on Monday 10 am, Room 4, agenda: line-2 downtime."
Courteous"Send it now.""Please send it by 4 pm so we can finish today."

Common mistake

Chasing courtesy and forgetting completeness - a polite message without the date or the part number still stops the work.

Method

  1. Name the purpose - what must the reader do?
  2. Write one sentence for that action.
  3. Add only the facts needed: what, where, when, how much.
  4. Close with a courteous request or a thank-you.

Worked example: the same message, rewritten

Before: "Respected sir, as per telephonic conversation with your good self, the material which was supposed to come has not come, so kindly do the needful at the earliest and oblige."

After: "Sir, the 12 mm MS plates promised on 5 March have not arrived. Please confirm dispatch today, as the job is stopped."

What changed

  • One paragraph of padding became two short sentences.
  • The vague 'material' became '12 mm MS plates'.
  • The date and the consequence (job stopped) were added.
  • The request is specific: confirm dispatch today.

Common mistake

Rewriting only the grammar. The weakness is usually missing facts, not missing politeness.

The model

S + E + C + D + R + N + F: Sender, Encoding, Channel, Decoding, Receiver, Noise, Feedback.

PartMeaningExample
Senderthe person with the ideathe supervisor
Encodingturning the idea into words or signschoosing the sentence
Channelthe route the message travelsa phone call
Decodingthe receiver interprets itthe fitter understands
Receiverthe person the message is forthe fitter
Noiseanything that disturbs the messagemachine noise on the line
Feedbackthe reply that closes the loop"Bearing checked, no play."

Read the model as a loop

Feedback puts the receiver back in the sender's place, so the loop closes and the next message starts from a shared understanding.

Common mistake

Learning the seven words without an example each. In an exam, one example per part is what earns the marks.

What encoding means

Encoding is choosing the symbols - words, numbers, gestures, drawings - that will carry the idea. Decoding is the receiver turning those symbols back into meaning.

Examples of encoding choices

The same idea, encoded three ways

  • "Torque to 45 N·m" - words and a number for a technician.
  • A torque wrench with a dial set at 45 - a visual and physical code.
  • A drawing with the symbol for 'tighten to 45 N·m' - a standard engineering code.

When decoding fails

SentUnderstoodWhy
"Check the bearing clearance."cleaned the bearingsimilar sound, careless listening
"Use the 6 mm bit."used the 6 inch bitunit dropped in speech
"Cut it 2 m long."cut it 2 feet longmixed units

Common mistake

Assuming the other person uses your code. Units, abbreviations and slang differ between trades and regions.

Channel choice is part of the message

The channel decides how fast the message travels, how much detail survives, and whether there is a record.

ChannelBest forExample
Face to faceinstruction, correction, bad newsexplaining a job to a new helper
Phone callurgent, short, needs an answer now"Stop the line, the guard is loose."
E-mailrecord, detail, attachmentsending a drawing revision to a vendor
Notice boardeveryone at once, rulesthe new safety helmet rule
Drawing or chartshapes, positions, quantitiesthe panel layout before wiring
WhatsApp groupquick coordination on site"Material reached gate 2."

One message, wrong channel

A 40-line specification sent as a voice note: it will be misheard and lost. The same text as an e-mail with a table is used for years.

Common mistake

Using the fastest channel for a message that needs a record, or the most formal channel for a question that needs an answer in one minute.

Noise

Noise is anything that reduces the fidelity of the message. It is not only sound.

Examples of noise

Type of noiseExample
Physicalcompressor running beside the phone
Technicala weak signal cutting half a sentence
Semanticjargon the receiver does not know
Psychologicalthe receiver is worried about a breakdown
Organisationalthe message passes through four people before it arrives

Feedback

Feedback can be verbal ("understood, 45 N·m"), written (a signed job card), or non-verbal (a nod, a completed task).

Examples of feedback that actually checks understanding

Better than "ok"

  • "So the pump runs for one hour, then we check the seal - right?"
  • "I will send the drawing by 4 pm and call you after the test."
  • A job card signed by the supervisor after the work is inspected.

Common mistake

Accepting silence as agreement. Silence is the absence of feedback, not proof of understanding.

Definition

Downward communication flows from a higher level to a lower level: management to supervisors to workers. Its purpose is to direct, inform and explain.

What travels down

Examples

  • An order: "Run line 2 this afternoon."
  • A circular: "Safety helmets compulsory from Monday."
  • A policy: "Overtime needs written approval."
  • A job instruction with a drawing.
  • Feedback on performance: "Your rejection rate has dropped to 0.5 %."

Strengths and risks

It is fast and carries authority. The risk is dilution - each level trims or rewords, and the last person hears a different message.

Example of dilution

Management: "Reduce material wastage by 10 % this quarter." Third level: "Don't waste material." The number has gone, so no one knows what to do.

Common mistake

Sending a downward message once, in one channel, and assuming it has been received.

Definition

Upward communication flows from a lower level to a higher level: workers to supervisors to management. Its purpose is to report, suggest and warn.

What travels up

Examples

  • A report: "Line 2 was down 45 minutes; belt replaced."
  • A suggestion: "A roller stand here would save two men."
  • A grievance: "The night shift has no drinking water."
  • A warning: "Stock of 6205 bearings will finish by Thursday."
  • A clarification question: "Do we hold the batch until the test report arrives?"

Why organisations need it

The people closest to the machine know the problems first. If upward flow is weak, management plans with old information.

Example of a blocked upward message

A fitter notices a crack but says nothing because "nobody listens". Three weeks later the coupling fails. The information existed; the channel did not.

Common mistake

Reporting only good news. Upward communication is most valuable when it carries bad news early.

Side by side

PointDownwardUpward
Directiontop to bottombottom to top
Purposeorder, inform, explainreport, suggest, warn
Typical formcircular, instruction, appraisalreport, grievance, suggestion box
Tonedirectiverespectful, factual
Riskdilution and distortionfiltering and fear
Example"Helmets compulsory from Monday.""Two helmets are missing in our section."

Both directions carry the same message

A policy goes down, and the confirmation comes back up. Without the return path, the sender never learns whether the policy arrived.

Common mistake

Calling every internal message 'downward'. Ask who writes to whom; the direction follows from that.

Fixes that work

  • Shorten the chain: fewer levels between the decision and the machine.
  • Use one channel per message, and confirm receipt.
  • Hold a two-minute shift handover in person.
  • Keep a suggestion register with visible responses.
  • Answer grievances within a stated time.

Examples of a fix in action

ProblemFixResult
Instructions reach the shop floor changeda one-page job card with the drawingsame message at every level
Workers never hear back on suggestionsa weekly note listing accepted ideasupward flow increases
Supervisors are flooded with e-mailsone daily digest at 9 amimportant messages are read

Common mistake

Adding another level to 'improve control'. Every extra level is another place where the message can change.

Definition

Verbal communication uses words, spoken or written. It is the type you use most, and the one that carries the detail.

Oral and written compared

PointOralWritten
Speedinstant, with toneslower to produce
Recordnone unless recordedpermanent and traceable
Feedbackimmediatedelayed
Best forquick decisions, corrections, discussionspecifications, orders, reports, contracts
Example"Hold the job, I am coming.""Job No. 118 is on hold pending inspection."

Examples in a workshop

Ten seconds of verbal communication

  • Spoken instruction: "Tighten the gland nut, not the body."
  • Written record: "Gland nut tightened, no leak after 30 minutes."
  • Spoken warning: "Stand clear, starting the motor."
  • Written rule: "Never open the panel without isolation."

Common mistake

Leaving an important instruction only in speech. If it must be remembered, write it.

Definition

Non-verbal communication passes meaning without words - through the body, the voice and the use of space.

Five channels with examples

ChannelMeaningExample
Kinesics (body movement)gesture, posturea thumbs-up after inspection; folded arms during a discussion
Proxemics (space)distance and territorystanding close to a machine to point at a fault
Paralanguagetone, pitch, speed, pause"Fine." said flatly means the opposite
Haptics (touch)physical contacta hand on the shoulder in encouragement
Chronemics (time)punctuality as a messagearriving late for a handover signals little respect for it

Why it matters

In face-to-face talk, the body carries a large share of the meaning. A supervisor who says "take your time" while looking at the clock is not believed.

Common mistake

Reading one gesture as a fixed truth. Arms folded may mean cold, not angry - look at the whole situation.

Definition

Visual communication uses images: drawings, charts, graphs, maps, signs, icons and colour codes.

Examples you already meet

VisualWhat it replaces
A wiring diagrama page of text about connections
A bar chart of monthly breakdownsa table of figures
A red sign with a crossed circle"Do not enter"
A Gantt chartparagraphs about the schedule
A floor plan with escape routesa written evacuation description

Why engineers rely on it

A drawing shows shape, position and size at once, in a way no sentence can. Standards (IS, ISO) exist so the same symbol means the same thing everywhere.

Examples of visual communication going wrong

When a picture misleads

  • A chart with a cut y-axis makes a 2 % rise look like a doubling.
  • A sign in a language the visitor cannot read.
  • A drawing without a revision number - two versions in use at once.

Common mistake

Assuming a picture is automatically clear. Every visual needs a caption, a scale and a date.

Definition

Interpersonal communication is communication between two people, or within a small group, where each can see and answer the other.

Features

  • Two-way and immediate.
  • Carries feeling as well as information.
  • Depends on listening, tone and body language.

Examples

Interpersonal moments at work

  • Explaining a mistake to a helper without humiliating him.
  • A five-minute conversation with a supplier on the phone.
  • A supervisor and an apprentice agreeing on the order of jobs.
  • Apologising to a customer for a late delivery.

Why the tone matters

"You did it wrong" closes the conversation; "Let us see why the bore is oversize" keeps it open and solves the problem.

Common mistake

Sending an interpersonal message by e-mail. Criticism, apology and encouragement work better face to face.

h.en: 5.5 Intrapersonal, extra personal and mass communication

body.en:
Intrapersonal

Intrapersonal communication is communication with yourself - thinking, self-talk, planning, rehearsing.

Examples

  • "Check the torque twice today."
  • Rehearsing a sentence before a phone call.
  • Writing a to-do list and reading it back.

Extra personal

Extra personal communication is between a human being and a non-human: an animal, a machine, or a system that answers.

Examples

  • Telling a dog to sit.
  • Talking to a machine that will not start.
  • Reading a sensor's beep as a message and answering by pressing stop.

Mass

Mass communication reaches a large, unknown audience at once through a medium: newspaper, radio, television, website, social media.

Examples

  • A plant's safety week campaign on the notice boards and the website.
  • A government advisory on the radio.
  • A company's recruitment post on LinkedIn.

Common mistake

Calling a notice board 'mass communication' when it serves forty workers. Mass means a large, scattered, anonymous audience.

h.en: 5.6 Choosing the type for the situation

body.en:
Method: match the type to the situation

Ask three questions - how urgent is it, how much detail must survive, and how many people must receive it? The answers pick the type.

SituationTypeWhy
Correcting a dangerous habitinterpersonal, verbal + non-verbalneeds tone, eye contact and immediate feedback
Announcing a new policy to 300 workersmass / downward writtensame words to everyone, with a record
Recording that a bearing was replacedwritten verbaltraceable later
Showing a crack to a colleaguevisual + verbalpointing shows it faster than describing it
Talking yourself through a startup sequenceintrapersonalno second person involved
Congratulating a teaminterpersonalfeeling must travel with the words

Rule of thumb

Urgent and personal - speak. Detailed and lasting - write. Shape or position - draw. Many people, one message - publish.

Worked examples

  • A guard rail is broken during the shift: speak to the supervisor at once (interpersonal, verbal) and log it the same evening (written).
  • A crack on a coupling: call the fitter, point at it (visual), then photograph it for the report.
  • A safety rule for 300 workers: a written circular plus a notice-board display (mass, visual).

Common mistake

Using one favourite type for everything. A team that writes everything wastes time; a team that only speaks keeps no record.

Definition

Physical barriers are conditions in the environment or the medium that stop the message travelling intact.

Examples

Noise, distance and equipment

  • Two machines running beside a conversation in which a torque figure is given.
  • A phone call made from a workshop instead of a quiet corner.
  • A weak network dropping the last words of a voice message.
  • A guard's whistle lost inside ear protection.
  • A handwritten note blurred by rain on a site board.

Cures

  • Move to a quiet place before giving a number.
  • Repeat the key figure and make the listener repeat it.
  • Put critical instructions in writing.
  • Use the right channel: a drawing for shape, a call for urgency.

Example of the cost

"20 thou" and "20 mm" sound alike through noise. The first is a tolerance, the second is scrap.

Common mistake

Shouting louder instead of changing the channel. Louder does not remove a language or noise problem.

Definition

Language barriers come from the words themselves: jargon, ambiguity, poor grammar, different meanings for the same word.

Examples

Language problemExample
Jargon"Fix the DOB and reset the VFD." to a first-year apprentice
Ambiguity"Send it tomorrow" - which tomorrow, and what is 'it'?
Wrong word"The pump is not working properly" instead of "the pump leaks at the seal"
Grammar"The bolts is loose" - the reader hesitates
False friendBritish "chips" means fried potatoes, American "chips" means crispsfoods
AbbreviationMS means mild steel here and Microsoft in an e-mail elsewhere

Cures

  • Define a term the first time you use it.
  • Prefer one short word to three long ones.
  • Give numbers with units.
  • Ask the receiver to state the instruction back.

Worked example

"Do the needful" is not English that carries meaning. "Replace the gasket and tighten to 20 N·m" does.

Common mistake

Using jargon to look expert. Jargon excludes the person who must act on the message.

Definition

Psychological barriers sit inside the people: fear, prejudice, stress, inattention, mistrust, or a fixed idea.

Examples

Inside the sender and the receiver

  • A helper does not report a mistake because he fears the supervisor's anger.
  • A supervisor stops listening to an operator he has decided is careless.
  • A technician is so anxious about a breakdown that he hears only the first sentence.
  • A manager's "suggestion" is received as a criticism.
  • Everyone agrees in the meeting, and nothing changes afterwards.

Cures

  • Separate the person from the problem: discuss the bore, not the person.
  • Ask what the other person understood before replying.
  • Keep bad news safe to report - reward early warnings.
  • Pause, breathe and finish the sentence before answering.

Example

Reporting a crack two days late costs a coupling. Reporting it in the first hour costs a chat.

Common mistake

Treating fear as a personal weakness. It is a communication barrier, and it is removed by behaviour, not by orders.

Cultural barriers

Cultural barriers arise when customs, values or gestures differ between people.

Examples

  • Direct "no" is rude in some cultures, so silence is used instead.
  • The same hand gesture can be friendly in one region and offensive in another.
  • Hierarchy: a junior may not correct a senior, even when the senior is wrong.
  • A festival greeting is expected before business in some regions.

Organisational barriers

Organisational barriers come from the structure: too many levels, unclear channels, overload, or a culture that does not listen.

Examples

  • Six signatures needed before a spare is ordered.
  • Workers are told of a change after the machine has moved.
  • Everyone copies everyone, and the important mail is lost.
  • A suggestion box that is never opened.

Cures

  • Flatten the chain and name one owner per message.
  • Fix a channel per purpose (safety, quality, stores).
  • Set a response time and keep it.
  • Train the team in listening, not only in tools.

Summary of the five families

BarrierFirst question to ask
PhysicalCan we hear and see each other?
LanguageDo we use the same words for the same thing?
PsychologicalIs either of us afraid, angry or tired?
CulturalDoes this gesture mean the same to both of us?
OrganisationalIs there a clear channel and one owner?

Common mistake

Blaming the receiver ("he does not listen") without checking the channel, the wording and the timing.

h.en: Practice 1. Define communication and name its four language skills.

body.en:
Communication is the exchange of ideas, information or feelings between two or more people so that the receiver understands what the sender meant.

The four language skills are listening, speaking, reading and writing (LSRW). Listening and reading are receptive; speaking and writing are productive.

Example: a technician listens to the handover, reads the drawing, tells the helper which tools to bring and writes the entry in the log book - all four skills in one day.

h.en: Practice 2. Explain the communication cycle with its seven parts.

body.en:
The cycle is S + E + C + D + R + N + F: Sender, Encoding, Channel, Decoding, Receiver, Noise and Feedback.

The sender has the idea, encodes it into words or signs, sends it through a channel such as a phone call, and the receiver decodes it. Noise can disturb any stage, and feedback closes the loop.

Example: the supervisor says "torque the head bolts to 45 N·m" (encode, channel = speech); the fitter repeats it back (feedback); a compressor running nearby is the noise.

h.en: Practice 3. What is the difference between hearing and listening?

body.en:
Hearing is the physical reception of sound by the ear; it happens whether or not you pay attention.

Listening is active: you pay attention, interpret and remember, and often reply.

Example: you hear the machine alarm and keep working (hearing); you hear it, stop the line and check the coolant level (listening).

h.en: Practice 4. When is communication called effective? Give one example in favour and one against.

body.en:
Communication is effective when the receiver's understanding matches the sender's intention, and the reply or action shows that it does.

Effective: "Stop the conveyor, the guard is loose." One machine, one action, one reason.

Ineffective: "Something seems wrong with the machine, maybe check it." No machine, no action, no urgency, so nothing happens until something breaks.

h.en: Practice 5. Name the seven Cs of effective communication with one example each.

body.en:
The seven Cs are clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete and courteous.

Weak to better: "Do the needful" becomes "replace the gasket and refit the cover" (clear). "At this point of time we are not in a position to supply" becomes "we cannot supply before Monday" (concise). "The motor is faulty" becomes "the motor draws 9 A against a rated 6 A" (concrete).

"The bolts is loose" becomes "the bolts are loose" (correct). A jumbled list is put in time order (coherent). "Meeting on Monday" gains a time, a room and an agenda (complete). "Send it now" becomes "please send it by 4 pm so we can finish today" (courteous).

h.en: Practice 6. Define downward communication and give three examples.

body.en:
Downward communication flows from a higher level to a lower level of an organisation - from management to supervisors to workers.

Its purpose is to direct, inform and explain. Examples: an order ("run line 2 this afternoon"), a circular ("safety helmets compulsory from Monday") and a policy ("overtime needs written approval").

The main risk is dilution: the number in "reduce wastage by 10 %" disappears by the time it reaches the shop floor.

h.en: Practice 7. Define upward communication and give three examples.

body.en:
Upward communication flows from a lower level to a higher level - from workers to supervisors to management.

Its purpose is to report, suggest and warn. Examples: a breakdown report ("line 2 down 45 minutes, belt replaced"), a suggestion ("a roller stand here would save two men") and a warning ("6205 bearings will finish by Thursday").

It is most valuable when it carries bad news early, as a fitter's report of a small crack prevents a coupling failure.

h.en: Practice 8. Differentiate between downward and upward communication.

body.en:
Downward flows from top to bottom; upward flows from bottom to top.

Downward carries orders, circulars, policy and instructions, in a directive tone; upward carries reports, suggestions, grievances and warnings, in a factual tone.

Examples: "helmets compulsory from Monday" goes down, and "two helmets are missing in our section" comes up. The risk of downward flow is dilution; the risk of upward flow is filtering through fear.

h.en: Practice 9. What is verbal communication? Compare its oral and written forms.

body.en:
Verbal communication uses words, either spoken or written.

Oral is instant, carries tone and gives immediate feedback, but leaves no record; written is slower, permanent and traceable, but feedback is delayed.

Examples: orally - "hold the job, I am coming"; in writing - "job no. 118 is on hold pending inspection". Details and orders belong in writing; quick corrections belong in speech.

h.en: Practice 10. Explain non-verbal communication with three examples.

body.en:
Non-verbal communication carries meaning without words, through the body, the voice and the use of space.

Kinesics: a thumbs-up after inspection shows approval. Paralanguage: a flat "fine" can mean the opposite of the word. Proxemics: standing close to a machine to point at a fault shows where the problem is.

Two more channels are haptics (touch, such as a hand on the shoulder) and chronemics (time - arriving late for a handover signals that it is not important).

h.en: Practice 11. Give two examples of visual communication and say why engineers use it.

body.en:
Visual communication uses drawings, charts, graphs, maps and signs.

Examples: a wiring diagram shows connections faster than a page of text, and a bar chart of monthly breakdowns shows a trend that a table of figures hides.

Engineers rely on it because a drawing carries shape, position and size at once, and because standard symbols (IS, ISO) mean the same thing to every reader - provided the drawing has a scale, a caption and a revision number.

h.en: Practice 12. Explain interpersonal, intrapersonal, extra personal and mass communication.

body.en:
Interpersonal is between two people or in a small group, two-way and immediate - a supervisor explaining a mistake to a helper.

Intrapersonal is with yourself - rehearsing a phone call or writing a to-do list. Extra personal is between a human being and a non-human - telling a dog to sit, or reading a sensor's beep as a message.

Mass reaches a large, scattered, anonymous audience through a medium - a newspaper, radio, website or social-media post.

h.en: Practice 13. Name the five families of barriers and give one example of each.

body.en:
Physical: two machines running beside a phone call in which a torque figure is given. Language: "fix the DOB and reset the VFD" to a first-year apprentice.

Psychological: a helper hides a mistake because he fears the supervisor's anger. Cultural: a junior will not correct a senior, even when the senior is wrong.

Organisational: six signatures are needed before a spare is ordered, so the machine stays down.

h.en: Practice 14. How can the barriers to communication be removed?

body.en:
First name the barrier, then remove its cause.

For physical barriers, move to a quiet place and confirm key figures back. For language barriers, define terms, use plain words and give numbers with units. For psychological barriers, make early reporting safe and discuss the problem rather than the person.

For cultural barriers, ask what a gesture means before judging it; for organisational barriers, shorten the chain, keep one owner per message and answer grievances within a stated time.

title.en: The communication cycle: S E C D R N F
The seven Cs of a good message

a.en: Sender → Encoding → Channel → Decoding → Receiver, with Noise throughout and Feedback closing the loop
the receiver's understanding equals the sender's intention
clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete, courteous
listening, speaking, reading, writing (LSRW)
top to bottom: orders, circulars, policy, instructions
bottom to top: reports, suggestions, grievances, warnings
words / body and voice / images and signs
between people / with yourself
with a non-human / with a large anonymous audience
noise, distance, weak signal, bad handwriting

q.en: What is communication?

a.en: The exchange of ideas, information or feelings between people so that the receiver understands what the sender meant.

q.en: What are the four language skills?

a.en: Listening and speaking (oral), reading and writing (written) - LSRW.

q.en: What is the difference between hearing and listening?

a.en: Hearing is the ear receiving sound; listening is paying attention, understanding and remembering.

q.en: When is communication called effective?

a.en: When the receiver's understanding matches the sender's intention and the reply or action shows it.

q.en: Name the seven Cs.

a.en: Clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete, courteous.

q.en: Give one example of ineffective communication and say why.

a.en: "Do the needful" - it names no action, no object and no time, so the reader cannot act on it.

q.en: Expand S+E+C+D+R+N+F.

a.en: Sender, Encoding, Channel, Decoding, Receiver, Noise, Feedback.

q.en: What is encoding? Give an example.

a.en: Turning an idea into words, numbers or signs - for example saying "torque to 45 N·m" instead of pointing at the bolt.

q.en: What is feedback and why is it important?

a.en: The receiver's reply or action; it closes the loop and proves the message arrived, for example "bearing checked, no play".

q.en: What is noise in communication?

a.en: Anything that reduces the fidelity of the message - machine noise, a weak signal, jargon, or a distracted receiver.

q.en: Define downward communication with two examples.

a.en: Message from a higher to a lower level: an order to run line 2, or a circular making helmets compulsory.

q.en: Define upward communication with two examples.

a.en: Message from a lower to a higher level: a breakdown report, or a suggestion about a roller stand.

q.en: Name the three main types of communication by medium.

a.en: Verbal (words), non-verbal (body and voice) and visual (images and signs).

q.en: Give an example of intrapersonal communication.

a.en: Talking yourself through a startup sequence, or writing a to-do list and reading it back.

q.en: What is mass communication?

a.en: Communication with a large, scattered, anonymous audience through a medium such as a newspaper, radio, website or social media.

q.en: Name the five families of barriers.

a.en: Physical, language (semantic), psychological, cultural and organisational.

q.en: Give a physical barrier and its cure.

a.en: Machine noise beside a phone call; the cure is to move to a quiet place and confirm the figure back.

q.en: Give a language barrier and its cure.

a.en: "Fix the DOB and reset the VFD" to an apprentice; the cure is to define the term or use plain words.

q.en: Give a psychological barrier and its cure.

a.en: A helper hides a mistake out of fear; the cure is to make early reporting safe and to discuss the problem, not the person.

q.en: How does an organisation create barriers?

a.en: Through too many levels, unclear channels, overload and a culture that does not answer suggestions.
